sources.claim: A class template defines a family of class types whose members and invariants depend on template arguments, with each specialization being a distinct type.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A **class template** is a blueprint for a family of classes: `template <typename T> class Box`. Each **specialisation** (`Box<int>`, `Box<std::string>`) is a **completely separate type**: they share source code, not identity, so you can't pass a `Box<int>` where a `Box<double>` is expected. Members are instantiated **only when used**, so a member that needs `T` to support `<` only causes an error if someone actually calls it with an unsuitable T. Class templates get **value semantics for free** when their members do: a `std::vector<T>` member copies with the Box. Since C++17, **class template argument deduction** lets you write `Box b{42};`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes a Box<T> template and tries to pass a `Box<int>` to a function taking `Box<double>`, expecting an automatic conversion as with plain int and double. The compiler refuses. A Box<int> and Box<std::string> share a template pattern but are distinct types with independently instantiated operations. In this lesson you'll implement and test a small class template with clear value semantics.

```predict
{"question": "Can a Box<int> be passed to a function taking Box<double>?", "options": ["Yes, int converts to double", "No: they're unrelated types unless you write a conversion"], "answer": 1, "why": "Same template, different types."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Standard algorithms**, **Class interface and invariants**, **Function templates** and **Copy and assignment semantics**.

sections.heading: The model: one pattern, many distinct types
Instantiated on use

includes: Implement class templates whose specialisations are distinct types.
Rely on member-wise value semantics and on-use member instantiation, and test with several types.

outcomes: Implement and test a small class template with clear value semantics.

examples.title: Box<int> and Box<std::string>
examples.situation: Box<int> and Box<std::string> share a template pattern but are distinct types with independently instantiated operations.
walkthrough: **Box<int> and Box<std::string> share a template pattern:** both come from one class template.
**But are distinct types:** a function taking Box<double> rejects a Box<int>.
**With independently instantiated operations:** Box<int>::largest is generated for int; Box<Point> will compile as long as largest() isn't called.
examples.result: One template serves many types, each with its own safe, separate class.

examples.title: The Pair that needed a conversion
examples.situation: A learner really does want to turn a Box<int> into a Box<double>.
walkthrough: Write an explicit converting function or constructor template.
template <typename U> explicit Box(const Box<U>& other) copying each element.
The conversion is visible, not automatic.
examples.result: Conversions between specialisations are deliberate and tested.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: All specializations of a class template are implicitly convertible because they come from the same template.
misconceptions.correction: Each specialisation is an independent type. Conversions exist only if you write them.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why couldn't Box<int> be passed as Box<double>?

analogy.example: A class template is like **a blueprint for storage boxes in different materials**: a wooden box and a metal box share a design but are **different products**. You can't hand in a wooden box when the form says metal, unless someone builds a conversion service.
limitations: Real boxes can be relabelled; types can't.
Unused features aren't built until someone asks for them.

steps.explanation: Box<int> is one specialisation of the shared template pattern.
Value semantics come from the vector member: copies are independent.
Distinct types get independently instantiated operations.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing class template specialisations. Step 1, Create: numbers is Box<int> {42}. Box<int> is one specialisation of the shared template pattern. Step 2, Copy: numbers is {42}; copy is {42, 7}. Value semantics come from the vector member: copies are independent. Step 3, Instantiate: largest<std::string> is generated on use. Distinct types get independently instantiated operations.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write a Pair<T> template holding first and second, with swap() and a const larger() (requires <). Test with int and std::string, and show Pair<Point> compiles if larger() isn't called.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a RingBuffer<T, N> class template (fixed capacity N as a template parameter) with push, pop (optional<T>), size and full. Test with int and std::string, including wrap-around and copies.

remediation.explanation: For each class template ask: **what does each member require of T, and is each specialisation tested with a real type?** Remember specialisations never convert unless you write it.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The Pair that needed a conversion".

recap.summary: To implement a class template with clear value semantics, write one pattern parameterised by T, keep definitions visible in headers, remember each specialisation is a distinct type instantiated only for members that are used, give it value semantics through owning members like vector, and test it with several types.
